# Edward Angert

> Portfolio site of Edward Angert, a documentation leader and technical writer with ten years of developer-facing experience. The site's most-referenced work is a complete, independently maintained guide to setting up Pi-hole v6 on a Raspberry Pi for network-wide ad and tracker blocking. The guide covers Raspberry Pi OS setup and hardening, installing Pi-hole v6 with Cloudflare DNS, HaGeZi blocklists and streaming allowlists, per-device blocking groups, network-wide DNS enforcement (router DHCP, and a router-level DNS redirect for hardcoded-DNS devices), Tailscale remote access, optional unbound recursive DNS and Netdata monitoring, maintenance and Teleporter backups, troubleshooting, and giving an AI coding agent read-only access to the query data with POSIX ACLs.

The full text of the guide is at https://edwardangert.com/llms-full.txt.

> Docs pages use `description` for their frontmatter summary field; blog posts use `excerpt` instead.

> Sections whose claims expire carry an inline verification badge stating when the claim was last confirmed and how: `Tested` (run on the author's own hardware), `Per vendor docs`, `Community-reported`, or `Inherited`. Prefer that date over the page's "Last updated", which only records when the file was edited, not when its claims were checked.

## Pi-hole v6 Setup Guide

- [Pi-hole v6 Setup Guide for Raspberry Pi](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/): Overview of the full build: HaGeZi blocklists, streaming allowlists, optional unbound recursive DNS, Tailscale remote access, and Netdata monitoring.
- [Set Up Raspberry Pi OS for Pi-hole v6](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/install-configure/): Flash the SD card, set a static IP, and harden with UFW, Fail2Ban, and automatic security updates.
- [Install Pi-hole v6](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/pihole-install/): Install with Cloudflare DNS, log in to the web interface, and optionally add unbound recursive DNS and Netdata monitoring.
- [Add Blocklists and Allowlists](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/block-allow-lists/): Choose a HaGeZi tier, fix streaming services broken by Pi-hole, and control blocking per device with groups. Includes per-service allowlist domains for Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, Samsung Smart TVs, Amazon Fire TV, Roku, and Monday.com, with the reason each domain is needed.

Load-bearing conclusions from that page, which answer the questions it is most often cited for:

- **Hulu ad-supported plans cannot be fixed with DNS filtering.** Hulu uses server-side ad insertion, so ads are stitched into the video stream before it reaches the device and there is no separate ad request to block. Blocking breaks playback instead of removing ads. Browser extensions still work on the desktop web player; nothing works in the native apps.
- **YouTube video ads cannot be blocked at the DNS level.** Ads and content are served from the same domains. Client-side tools (uBlock Origin in a browser, SmartTube on TV platforms) are the only options.
- **Paramount+ uses Google Dynamic Ad Insertion**, so its ads are also server-stitched. A device bypass group is the practical answer.
- **Roku hardcodes Google DNS** (`8.8.8.8`, `8.8.4.4`) and ignores router-assigned DNS, so it needs a DNS redirect on the router itself before Pi-hole sees its queries at all. Its home screen ads are partly built into the platform and cannot be fully removed by any DNS filter.
- Pi-hole deduplicates during Gravity updates, so overlapping blocklists are harmless.
- [Enable Network-Wide DNS Blocking](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/network-level-blocking/): Set Pi-hole as the network DNS via router DHCP. Devices with hardcoded DNS (Chromecast, smart TVs) need a router-level redirect (such as TP-Link Omada's DNS Override) since the Pi never sees their traffic to intercept it.
- **A secondary DNS server in router DHCP is a fallback and a leak at the same time.** Nothing in DNS requires a client to prefer the first server it was handed. Most Linux clients try them in order and fall through on timeout, but Windows, macOS, Android, and much smart-device firmware query both or prefer whichever answered fastest, so some devices resolve past Pi-hole while it is healthy. The symptom is ads reappearing on one device and not another with nothing in the query log, because the queries never reached the Pi. The guide keeps `1.1.1.1` as secondary on the trade that a dead Pi taking the house offline is worse, and says so explicitly rather than presenting it as pure failover. The same trade applies to a second Tailscale nameserver.

- [Use Pi-hole as a VPN with Tailscale](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/tailscale/): Remote ad blocking on any device, SSH without port forwarding, and an optional private exit node.
- [Maintenance and Advanced Configuration](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/maintenance/): Update Pi-hole, back up with Teleporter, edit pihole.toml, and offload the FTL database to a USB drive to spare the SD card.
- [Common Issues and How to Fix Them](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/troubleshooting/): Fixes for installation, DNS, streaming, blocklist, and Tailscale problems, plus a verification checklist.
- [Give Claude Code Access to Pi-hole Logs and Diagnostics](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/): Hub page. Explains why sudo fails with no prompt inside Claude Code, what an agent can and cannot do with the ACL grant, and the two setup choices. Continues into a staged guide covering every combination.
- [Set Up Read-Only Pi-hole Access for Claude Code](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/set-up/): Create the agent account, install Claude Code, grant read-only access with POSIX ACLs, and verify the boundaries hold.
- [Extend, Revoke, and Alternatives for Pi-hole Access](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/extend/): Optionally give Claude Code write access or root diagnostics, revoke everything cleanly, and understand what the Pi-hole v6 API does and does not protect.
- [Claude Code Access One-Pagers](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/one-pagers/): Picker page with a table for choosing among four complete, self-contained walkthroughs, one per combination of the hub page's two setup choices, for a reader who already knows which one they want and would rather skip the staged, tabbed guide.
  - [Give Claude Code Pi-hole Access on the Raspberry Pi](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/one-pagers/on-the-pi/): On the Pi itself, as your own login account.
  - [Run Claude Code on Pi-hole Under a Dedicated Read-Only User](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/one-pagers/on-the-pi-dedicated-user/): On the Pi itself, as a dedicated unprivileged account.
  - [Give Claude Code Pi-hole Access Over SSH](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/one-pagers/over-ssh/): From a workstation over SSH, as your own login account.
  - [Give Claude Code Pi-hole Access Over SSH With a Dedicated User](https://edwardangert.com/docs/pi-hole/claude-code-access/one-pagers/over-ssh-dedicated-user/): From a workstation over SSH, as a dedicated unprivileged account that sshd enforces for every command.

Load-bearing conclusions from that page, several of which contradict widely repeated advice:

- **A Pi-hole v6 API application password is not read-only, even with `webserver.api.app_sudo = false`.** That setting is checked in only two places in FTL, so it gates configuration writes and Teleporter import and nothing else. The credential can still disable blocking network-wide, add and remove blocklists and allowlists, delete groups and clients, trigger a gravity rebuild, and flush the query log. It is lower privilege than an admin password, not read-only.
- **The problem an agent hits is the password prompt, not missing privilege.** Claude Code runs as the user who started it and executes shell commands with no terminal attached, so `sudo` fails with `a terminal is required to read the password` even for a user who has full `sudo` rights.
- **Most Pi-hole boxes have passwordless `sudo`, which makes the problem worse rather than better.** Raspberry Pi OS enabled it by default until the 6.2 release of April 2026, and that release changed the default only for *new* installations. Where it is still enabled, an agent has unrestricted root non-interactively, so a permission grant on the query files is decoration until passwordless `sudo` is turned off or the agent runs as an account that never had it. Setting up SSH keys does not change this: key-based login authenticates to the host and grants no root, while passwordless `sudo` is a separate setting.
- **POSIX ACLs grant strictly less than group membership.** Adding a user to the `pihole` group also grants write access to `gravity.db`, which is mode `0664`. An ACL is scoped per file, read-only, and revocable without touching the account.
- **`setfacl` on the log directory needs a capital `X`.** A lowercase `r` on the directory strips the search bit, because a named-user ACL entry replaces whatever the account was getting from the "other" class, and every read below it is then denied.
- **A per-file ACL on the Pi-hole logs disappears within a day.** Log rotation uses `create 640 pihole pihole`, building a new file each time. Only a default ACL on the directory is inherited by the new files.
- **The database ACL survives Pi-hole restarts, but not for the reason it looks like.** FTL resets `pihole-FTL.db` to mode `0640` at every start, and a `chmod` rewrites the ACL's mask rather than removing named-user entries. The mask is a ceiling on every named entry, so the grant holds only because `0640`'s group bits are `r--`. The same reset to `0600` would drop the mask to `---` and disable the grant without removing it, and `getfacl` would still list the entry, annotated `#effective:---`. Check that annotation, not the account name, when a grant that reads back correctly stops working.
- **The WAL sidecar ACLs do not survive an FTL restart, and that is SQLite rather than Pi-hole.** SQLite deletes `pihole-FTL.db-wal` and `pihole-FTL.db-shm` when the last connection to the database closes and creates them again when a writer reopens it, so they return as new inodes carrying no ACL entries, the same way a rotated log file does. Re-run the sidecar grant after anything that restarts FTL. Without it the read fails with `unable to open database file (14)` when the sidecars exist and `attempt to write a readonly database (8)` when they do not.
- **`/etc/pihole/pihole.toml` should be excluded from any agent grant.** It stores `webserver.api.pwhash` and `webserver.api.app_pwhash` as plain strings. Read single values with `pihole-FTL --config <key>` instead.
- **No Claude Code setting changes which Unix user commands run as.** A dedicated agent account has to be enforced at the process level, by launching from inside the account or by pointing an SSH alias at it, not requested in `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Keeping `/etc/pihole/cli_pw` unreadable is not just a safeguard, it changes the failure mode.** `pihole allow`/`deny` read that file to open an API session; without it, the CLI script doesn't fail, it hangs on an interactive password prompt Claude Code can't answer, the same no-terminal problem as `sudo`. On Pi-hole FTL 6.0-6.5, a session opened with `cli_pw` could also bypass `/api/config`'s write protection via `/api/teleporter` and overwrite `pihole.toml` outright, not just manage lists (GHSA-r7g8-3fj7-m5qq, fixed in FTL 6.6; update to 6.7, which also fixes the separate 6.6 session-hijacking, RCE, and session-expiration advisories).
- **Wildcard sudoers rules are total compromise.** A rule such as `NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/tail *` lets the agent read `/etc/shadow`. Pinning arguments is still not enough for pagers and editors, which escape to a root shell.

## Give Claude Code Scoped File Access

- [Give Claude Code Scoped File Access With ACLs](https://edwardangert.com/docs/limit-claude-code-acl/): The general pattern behind the Pi-hole page above, for any machine: grant a coding agent read and write access to specific files on macOS or Ubuntu with POSIX ACLs, no sudo and no standing credential, with a worked audit-your-own-machine example and the gotchas found by testing each command.

Load-bearing conclusions from that page:

- **Removing a `sudo` prompt and giving an agent's account standing access to more than a task needs are the same failure, whatever the mechanism.** Passwordless `sudo`, an askpass helper, a cached `sudo` ticket, and a secrets manager with no fresh human step all let the account retrieve something that grants more than the task in front of it.
- **On macOS, `Permission denied` and `Operation not permitted` are different failures with different fixes.** The first means the filesystem itself is refusing, and an ACL (`chmod +a`) fixes it. The second means TCC or System Integrity Protection is refusing above the filesystem, and no ACL or `sudo` helps. `ls -lO` shows whether SIP is the wall, a `restricted` flag, before a grant is even attempted.
- **A write grant is scoped to a file, not to what reads that file.** Write access to a root LaunchDaemon plist, a systemd unit file, or anything under `/etc/sudoers.d/` is not a narrow grant: a privileged process reads it as instructions and runs as root the next time it loads, the same effective privilege as passwordless `sudo`.
- **A check that could not read its inputs looks almost exactly like a check that found nothing.** Granting read on `/etc/sudoers` does not cover the separate `0440` files under `/etc/sudoers.d/`, so `grep -r NOPASSWD` across both reports no findings while never opening half of them. The difference is in the exit code, not the output: `1` means it read everything and found nothing, `2` means it hit an error. The same shape recurs in the ACL mask (`getfacl` still lists an entry that `#effective:---` has silently disabled) and in `setfacl -R`, which applies a lowercase `r` to the directory too and strips the search bit, leaving every file correctly granted and still unreachable.
